To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

near surface radionuclide concentration (in particular radon-222) is more closely tied than wind speed to atmospheric mixing depth and that this relationship can be used to improve the performance of source apportionment techniques such as ME-2.

1) the radon-based implementation out-performs the wind speed implementation of ME-3, 2) this is due to the more direct relationship between near-surface radon concentration and atmospheric mixing depth, 3) the performance of the ME-2 implementation is affected by the distribution of sources and 4) the radon signal is most useful for sources whose concentrations are most directly tied to atmospheric mixing.

(1) The diurnal signal in radon concentrations can be used as an indicator of atmospheric mixing depth for source apportionment in ME-2; (2) The diurnal radon concentration signal is more effective than wind speed in improving the source apportioning of primary aerosol emissions in a small rural setting with a relatively low concentration of anthropogenic aerosols; and (3) The diurnal timescale is a significant contributor to the variability of near surface atmospheric radon concentration.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new approach to the application of ME-2, and the results of this study suggest that it is a promising avenue of future research.
the development and evaluation of a new approach for the source apportioning of fine atmospheric particulates (PM_(2,5)).
the development of a method to improve source apportionment for fine PM_(2.3) by using near-surface measurements of radon-222 as a proxy for atmospheric mixing depth.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the radon-based version of ME-2 is more accurate than the wind-based version, but only in certain cases, and that the accuracy of both versions of ME- 2 is affected by the distribution of source types and the nature of the source apportioned aerosol.
the use of near surface radon concentrations as a proxy for mixing depth in ME-2 improves the source apportioned results, particularly for the finer primary aerosol sources.

the radon-based approach to ME-2 is more effective at reproducing daily source contributions than the wind speed approach, and this is particularly the case for sources that are more directly tied in their concentration to atmospheric mixing depth.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
radon-based ME2 can provide a more accurate source apportionment than the wind speed version of the ME2 model, and that the radon-based version is more robust in the presence of calm wind conditions.

(1) the radon-based version of ME-2 is more successful than the wind speed based version for the township of Muswellook, and (2) the performance of multi linear models for source apportionment is affected by the distribution and characteristics the aerosol sources.

(1) the radon-based implementation improved the source apportionments for primary sources, and (2) the wind speed-based implementation was more successful in reproducing source contributions from the secondary source types (Sulphate, Ammonia and Nitrate).
The main takeaway from our work is that

near-surface radon concentration is a useful proxy for atmospheric mixing depth in source apportionment studies, particularly for rural or industrial sites with significant contributions from primary emissions.
the radon signal can be used to improve source apportionment in ME-2 when the source distribution is dominated by primary emissions that are more easily lifted and suspended.
the diurnal timescale radon signal is more closely related to atmospheric mixing depth and therefore pollutant concentrations than the daily timescale wind speed signal.
